To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the serotonin transporter (Sert) gene interacts in complex ways with the dopamine transporter (DAT) gene, the norepinephrine transporter (NET) gene, the monoamine oxidase A (MaOa) gene, the 5‐HT(1B) receptor gene (Htr1b) and the brain derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) gene.

heterozygous or homozygous gene knockout mice can provide relevant models of human polygenic and/or epistatic traits, and that such models can be used to study interactions between genes that have not previously been studied together in human studies.

the SERT knockout phenotype can be altered by the presence or absence of other genetic variants, such that the resulting phenotypes can be synergistic, additive, antagonistic or more complex, depending on the particular combination of variants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of gene–gene and gene‐environment interactions that can be used as experimental models for the genetic and molecular basis of complex human traits and disorders.
the study of gene–gene and gene–environment interactions, including epigenetic effects, in mouse behavioral and neurobiological phenotypes.

understanding gene interactions that may contribute to the development of complex human traits and disorders, and the ways in which the results of our research may help in the development of new and better treatments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the interactions between SERT and other genes are complex and quantitative.
there are no definitive conclusions, but there is much promise for further studies.
the interactions between variations of the expression of SERT and other genes can be quite complex, and may be better understood in terms of quantitative rather than binary alterations.

, for the six mouse genes studied, gene–gene interaction studies can provide a variety of phenotypic models that could be relevant for understanding human gene–gene interactions and their roles in the etiology of complex disorders.
the interactions among SERT and these five other genes are more complicated than the simple additive interactions that are usually assumed to be present in complex traits.
gene–gene interactions can be studied in mice and can be informative, but that the results can be complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of interactions between SERT and other genes can be used to develop a better understanding of how gene interactions may affect complex human phenotypes.
the experimental studies of gene–gen interactions in mice can provide a useful approach for understanding the genetic complexity of human disorders and for developing new therapeutic strategies.
experimental models of gene–gene and gene–environment interactions can be useful for identifying the molecular genetic bases for human disorders.
